The problem: verified text is not yet training input A matching checksum tells us which text we have, not whether every record should enter a training corpus. A record may be malformed, too large for the processing budget, or contain a literal marker that our chosen policy excludes. Some records need review rather than an automatic yes or no. Deleting every excluded record without keeping its reason loses useful evidence. Reporting only the final retained count also hides which records each rule actually examined. If an early rule stops a record, later rules cannot truthfully report that the record passed or failed them. The solution here is an ordered filter with three dispositions: Retained: a candidate for the next data-processing stage, not a guarantee of quality, privacy or permission. Rejected: excluded by an automatic rule. Manual review: withheld from downstream training input. This example has no approval override. The first rule in the configured order that rejects a record or holds it for manual review supplies that record’s first terminal decision. Evaluation stops there; later rules are not evaluated for that record. If a record survives every rule, it is retained with no first terminal rule. The report preserves each record’s disposition, the rules actually evaluated, any first terminal rule and the record’s reference to its raw source. It does not copy excluded text into public findings.
Eight records, with explicit boundaries Everything in the worked example is course-authored synthetic data. It is not a filtering result for TinyStories. The two source names fixture-train and fixture-validation preserve their raw-source provenance; they do not create the final training, validation or test split. The selected framing policy, end-of-input-delimited-v2, recognizes the ASCII marker <|endoftext|> only when it occupies an entire physical line. A marker line may end with LF, CRLF or end of input. Its bytes are a delimiter, not payload text. The same marker inside an ordinary text line is not a delimiter. End of input also closes a remaining nonempty payload, even without a final newline. End of input immediately after a separator creates no extra record. Consecutive separators create an empty payload that the filter can reject. A failed read is an error, not an end-of-input boundary. These rules are selected explicitly; the reader does not guess another format after a failure. For this fixture, append b"<|endoftext|>
" after every record below, in table order within each source. Every separator therefore contributes 14 bytes. In Rust literals, 
 denotes one LF byte and \xff one byte that is invalid as standalone UTF-8. Label | Source | Complete raw payload construction | Payload bytes | First terminal decision r0 | fixture-train | b"cat sat.
" | 9 | None; retained r1 | fixture-train | b"\xff
" | 2 | Strict UTF-8; rejected r2 | fixture-train | 65 copies of b'x', then b"
" | 66 | Raw size; rejected r3 | fixture-train | b"hi
" | 3 | Minimum normalized length; rejected r4 | fixture-validation | b"....
" | 5 | Minimum ASCII letters; rejected r5 | fixture-validation | b"demo-key=CANARY
" | 16 | Secret marker; rejected r6 | fixture-validation | b"contact=alex@example.invalid
" | 29 | Manual marker; held r7 | fixture-validation | b"demo-key=CANARY contact=alex@example.invalid
" | 45 | Secret marker; rejected The marker text and address are fictional inputs. Their presence in this table explains the lesson; it is not permission to include captured secrets or personal data in a real findings report.
The solution: stop once, count at every reached rule The fixture deliberately uses small thresholds so each failure is visible: Reject a raw payload above 64 bytes before decoding it. Reject invalid UTF-8. Normalize the decoded text and reject fewer than 4 normalized UTF-8 bytes. Reject fewer than 1 ASCII letter. Reject the literal demo-key=CANARY, matched without ASCII case distinctions. Hold the literal contact=, matched case-sensitively. Hold text below the configured ASCII-letter share. Normalization replaces CRLF pairs with LF, then trims only space, tab, CR and LF at the two edges. It preserves case, internal spaces and other Unicode characters. Length after normalization is measured in UTF-8 bytes, not characters or tokens. For the last rule, count Unicode scalar values other than the six ASCII whitespace characters: space, tab, LF, vertical tab, form feed and CR. The numerator counts ASCII letters among those values. Compare a configured fraction using checked integer cross-products, rather than rounding a floating-point ratio. A zero denominator is unavailable and sends a reached record to review; it is not an observed share of zero. The fixture’s threshold is 0/1, so its last survivor passes this rule. These thresholds are not the full-corpus policy. The planned corpus policy uses a 65{,}536-byte raw limit, at least 16 normalized bytes, at least 8 ASCII letters and an ASCII-letter share of at least 1/2, with its own selected marker lists. For example, the fixture’s short secret record would reach a different first terminal rule under a stricter length threshold. None of the fixture’s rates are measurements of a real corpus. For a named rule k, report its terminal fraction using the population that actually reached it: r_k= rac{n_{\mathrm{disposition},k}}{n_{\mathrm{seen},k}}
Symbols in the filtering fraction k identifies a rule in the configured order. n_{\mathrm{seen},k} counts records surviving every earlier rule and reaching rule k. n_{\mathrm{disposition},k} counts reached records whose first terminal decision is rejection or a hold for review at rule k. r_k is dimensionless. When n_{\mathrm{seen},k}=0, the report stores unavailable, not zero. Four records reach the secret-marker rule, and it rejects two. Its terminal fraction is 2/4=1/2. Dividing by the original eight records gives 2/8=1/4, a different quantity: that rule’s terminal decisions as a fraction of all input records. Do not label the second quantity as the reached-population rate. The reached populations are 8,7,6,5,4,2,1, leaving one retained record. The final dispositions must conserve the input count: 8=1_{\mathrm{retained}}+6_{\mathrm{rejected}}+1_{\mathrm{manual\ review}} A binary exclusion summary gives 7 ineligible records, but those are 6 rejections plus 1 pending review. Calling all seven “rejected” discards the distinction needed to explain their outcomes.
Rust owns the framing and decisions The framer accepts an ordinary Read source. The output interface separates retained rows from body-free exclusion findings, without requiring a directory, filename, HTTP source or storage backend. Supporting libraries provide JSON encoding and SHA-256; the course code owns boundaries, rule order, terminal decisions and accounting. A bounded buffer retains only payloads within the selected size limit. An oversized record is drained to its boundary and counted without retaining its whole body. Read-buffer boundaries do not split records or invalidate a Unicode character: UTF-8 decoding happens on the complete bounded payload. Read the selected raw source completely and check its byte count and digest after framing. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/stream.rs#source-bound-framing pub fn scan_source<R: Read, F>( reader: R, source: &SourceBinding, policy: &FramingPolicy, mut visit: F, ) -> Result<ScanSummary, DataError> where F: FnMut(Frame) -> Result<(), DataError>, { policy.validate()?; let limit = source.bytes().checked_add(1).ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; let mut reader = reader.take(limit); let mut buffer = [0_u8; STREAM_BUFFER_BYTES]; let mut hasher = Sha256::new(); let mut observed = 0_u64; let mut framer = Framer::new(policy)?; loop { let length = reader.read(&mut buffer)?; if length == 0 { break; } observed = observed .checked_add(length as u64) .ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; if observed > source.bytes() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } hasher.update(&buffer[..length]); for &byte in &buffer[..length] { framer.feed(byte, &mut visit)?; } } framer.finish(&mut visit)?; if observed != source.bytes() || format!("{:x}", hasher.finalize()) != source.file_sha256() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } Ok(framer.summary) } The raw source was selected independently before this read. A report succeeds only after the complete source’s observed length and digest agree with that selection. Rows emitted before that final check are provisional. A changed byte, truncated read or I/O error prevents publication of the completed result; a prefix must not become training input. Replace each CRLF pair with LF, then trim only space, tab, CR and LF from both text edges; preserve the remaining text. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/filter.rs#narrow-normalization pub fn normalize(text: &str) -> String { text.replace("
", "
") .trim_matches([' ', '	', '
', '
']) .to_owned() } For one record, evaluate the configured rules in order and stop at its first rejection or manual-review decision. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/filter.rs#ordered-record-filter pub fn evaluate(frame: &Frame, policy: &FilterPolicy) -> Result<Decision, DataError> { policy.validate()?; let raw_bytes = frame.raw_bytes()?; let mut visited = vec![Rule::RawSize]; if raw_bytes > policy.framing.max_payload_bytes { return Ok(Decision::terminal(raw_bytes, visited, Rule::RawSize, None)); } let bytes = match &frame.data { FrameData::Bytes(bytes) if bytes.len() as u64 == raw_bytes => bytes, _ => return Err(DataError::InvalidRecord("frame body/span disagreement")), }; visited.push(Rule::Utf8); let text = match std::str::from_utf8(bytes) { Ok(text) => normalize(text), Err(_) => return Ok(Decision::terminal(raw_bytes, visited, Rule::Utf8, None)), }; let normalized_bytes = text.len() as u64; for &rule in &policy.stages[2..] { visited.push(rule); if normalized_terminal(&text, rule, policy)? { return Ok(Decision::terminal( raw_bytes, visited, rule, Some(normalized_bytes), )); } } Ok(Decision { disposition: Disposition::Retained, evaluated_rules: visited, first_terminal_rule: None, normalized_bytes: Some(normalized_bytes), raw_decoded: true, raw_bytes, retained_text: Some(text), }) } Record r7 contains both markers. With the secret rule first, it is rejected there; the manual-marker rule is not evaluated for that record. Swap those two rules and r7 is held for review instead. The new totals are one retained, five rejected and two pending review. The same raw bytes therefore produce different reasons and dispositions under different policies. Match secret-marker literals without ASCII case distinctions and manual-review literals case-sensitively; neither rule detects all sensitive text. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/privacy.rs#literal-marker-decisions pub fn contains_ascii_case_insensitive(text: &str, markers: &[String]) -> bool { markers.iter().any(|marker| { !marker.is_empty() && text .as_bytes() .windows(marker.len()) .any(|window| window.eq_ignore_ascii_case(marker.as_bytes())) }) } pub fn contains_case_sensitive(text: &str, markers: &[String]) -> bool { markers .iter() .any(|marker| !marker.is_empty() && text.contains(marker)) } A quoted marker can cause a false positive. Sensitive text without a configured literal can pass. Likewise, few ASCII letters do not prove that a record is bad or that it is not English, and many ASCII letters do not establish language or quality. These heuristics need corpus-specific inspection, including inspection of excluded text under appropriate access controls.
Preserve counts without exposing excluded bodies Increment a rule's seen count only when the record reaches it, then count survival or its first terminal decision. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/governance.rs#stage-accounting fn record(&mut self, decision: &Decision, record_id: &str) -> Result<(), DataError> { for &rule in &decision.evaluated_rules { let stage = self .stages .iter_mut() .find(|stage| stage.rule == rule) .ok_or(DataError::InvalidRecord("unknown evaluated stage"))?; add(&mut stage.seen, 1)?; if decision.first_terminal_rule == Some(rule) { add(&mut stage.terminal, 1)?; } else { add(&mut stage.survived, 1)?; } } if decision.raw_decoded { add(&mut self.decoded_raw_bytes, decision.raw_bytes)?; } else { add(&mut self.undecoded_raw_bytes, decision.raw_bytes)?; } let normalized = decision.normalized_bytes.unwrap_or(0); add(&mut self.normalized_bytes, normalized)?; match decision.disposition { Disposition::Retained => { add(&mut self.retained, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_retained_bytes, normalized)?; } Disposition::Rejected => { add(&mut self.rejected, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_rejected_bytes, normalized)?; } Disposition::ManualReview => { add(&mut self.manual_review, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_manual_bytes, normalized)?; } } let sample = self .samples .iter_mut() .find(|group| { group.disposition == decision.disposition && group.first_terminal_rule == decision.first_terminal_rule }) .ok_or(DataError::InvalidRecord("sample group"))?; if sample.record_ids.len() < SAMPLE_REFERENCES_PER_GROUP { sample.record_ids.push(record_id.to_owned()); } Ok(()) } A finding contains a source reference, half-open raw byte span, occurrence ID, evaluated rule IDs and the terminal decision. It contains no excluded body, snippet or matched capture. The occurrence ID binds the selected raw artifact, source and payload IDs, raw file digest and span. Equal text at different spans has different occurrence IDs. A changed filter policy does not change those raw occurrence IDs, but does change the derived artifact’s policy identity. Per source and terminal reason, the report includes the first 32 occurrence IDs in input order as samples. The full finding stream and counters remain complete: the sample bound is not permission to stop counting. Findings and the receipt share a strict metadata budget below 100 MiB. Exceeding that budget fails the attempt; it does not silently truncate evidence. Byte accounting uses separate bases. Separator bytes are outside raw payload spans. Payloads rejected before decoding still contribute to the raw total. Normalized byte totals include only records actually decoded and normalized. A complete run reads 287 physical bytes: 175 payload bytes and 112 delimiter bytes. Of the payload bytes, 68 belong to records rejected before decoding and 107 are decoded. Normalization leaves 101 bytes across decoded records: 8 retained, 65 rejected and 28 pending review. These are byte counts, not token counts; excluded text still contributes to its applicable accounting totals. A retained row is checked again against the selected filtered artifact, policy, source references, span and text digest before consumption. Relabeling a manual-review payload or selecting an untrusted candidate’s own manifest does not make it eligible. Run the offline synthetic fixture and print the report derived from the Rust decisions. rust/demos/ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering/src/main.rs#offline-filtering-example fn main() { match ch42_deterministic_corpus_filtering::demo_report().and_then(|report| { serde_json::to_string_pretty(&report).map_err(|_| { llm_from_scratch::functional::data::stream::DataError::InvalidRecord( "report serialization", ) }) }) { Ok(report) => println!("{report}"), Err(error) => { eprintln!("filter fixture failed: {error}"); std::process::exit(1); } } } To reproduce the example, start at the repository root with Docker installed and the course development image available. This command uses only synthetic bytes, so the corpus download is disabled: COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering The JSON report records eight inputs, one retained record, six rejected records and one pending-review record, plus each rule’s reached count and terminal fraction. Its changed-order comparison records one retained, five rejected and two pending review. Artifact digests identify the actual policy and source bytes; do not replace them with illustrative hashes.
History: inspect what filtering removes A binary keep/drop report hides the reason for exclusion and the population that each later rule actually inspected. The C4 study examines text removed by filters; RefinedWeb later combines filtering and deduplication in a web-scale corpus. Dodge and colleagues inspect C4 exclusions and find disproportionate removal of content concerning minority groups by its word blocklist. Their 2021 Documenting Large Webtext Corpora: A Case Study on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus motivates examining removals rather than assuming that a filter is neutral. Penedo and colleagues describe a large web corpus built with filtering and deduplication, and evaluate language models trained on its data. Their 2023 RefinedWeb paper concerns a much broader pipeline than this eight-record fixture. Its model results do not certify our heuristics or isolate a benefit from one rule. The Rust contrast below is course-local: it reduces our existing decisions to one exclusion bit. It is not an implementation reproduced from either paper. It counts seven excluded records but loses their rejection-versus-review distinction and cannot say which later rule saw each one. Reduce the fixture's three dispositions to one exclusion bit and expose the information that summary omits. rust/demos/ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering/src/lib.rs#binary-filter-contrast /// A course-local reporting contrast, not either paper's implementation. pub fn binary_exclusion(disposition: Disposition) -> bool { disposition != Disposition::Retained } Record explicit exclusions and stage populations before deduplication and training; a passed heuristic is not a quality, privacy or memorization guarantee.
See the shrinking population First-terminal filtering of eight synthetic records Each rule sees only survivors of earlier rules. The secret-marker rule rejects two of its four inputs; record r7 stops there, so the later manual-marker rule is not evaluated for that record. Optional practice: inspect the recorded evidence Source withdrawal is a known-lineage calculation Filtering also preserves source lineage so a later withdrawal can identify recorded downstream artifacts. The separate fictional graph uses r0 as a raw-source node alias, not as the worked table’s record label or an actual occurrence digest. Its descendants are a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0. Two paths reach w0; the result lists it once. The unrelated branch f9 belongs to a different source and is not in this withdrawal’s descendant set. Validate the supplied lineage graph, then list each known descendant of the selected raw source once; this does not erase stored data. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/deletion.rs#known-descendant-withdrawal pub fn withdrawal( &self, raw_roots: &[String], limits: GraphLimits, ) -> Result<WithdrawalPlan, DataError> { let kinds = self.validate(limits)?; let mut reached = BTreeSet::new(); let mut pending = BTreeSet::new(); for root in raw_roots { if kinds.get(root.as_str()) != Some(&NodeKind::RawSource) { return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown or non-source root")); } pending.insert(root.as_str()); } while let Some(id) = pending.pop_first() { if !reached.insert(id) { continue; } for edge in &self.edges { if edge.parent == id && !reached.contains(edge.child.as_str()) { pending.insert(edge.child.as_str()); } } } let mut artifacts = Vec::new(); let mut sources = Vec::new(); for id in reached { match kinds.get(id) { Some(NodeKind::RawSource) => sources.push(id.into()), Some(NodeKind::Artifact) => artifacts.push(id.into()), None => return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown reached node")), } } Ok(WithdrawalPlan { artifacts, sources }) } Run these commands from the repository root with Docker installed and running. Each selects exactly one test; expect one passing test, not zero selected tests. Reproduce the fixture’s byte accounting. Inspect the assertions linking payload, delimiter, decoded and normalized byte totals. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering fixture_counts_and_byte_conservation -- --exact Reproduce the comparison that places the manual-marker rule before the secret-marker rule. Inspect the first terminal decision for r7 and the identities compared by the test. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering swapping_secret_and_review_changes_first_terminal -- --exact Reproduce the known-lineage withdrawal. Inspect the assertions checking the sorted, duplicate-free descendant set. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering withdrawal_reaches_known_descendants_once -- --exact Checked explanations for the three reproduction tasks The trailing LF byte in each decoded fixture payload remains part of the raw payload and physical source byte counts, but normalization trims it from the end of the decoded text. Internal LF characters remain unchanged. Trimming the trailing LF changes the normalized byte count, not the number of bytes read from the raw source. With the secret-marker rule first, r7 is rejected and never reaches the manual-marker rule. With the manual-marker rule first, r7 is held for review and never reaches the secret-marker rule. The raw source and occurrence identities do not change. The derived policy and artifact identities change because the ordered filtering policy is different. The descendant set contains a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0, with w0 listed once despite its two incoming paths; it excludes the unrelated f9. This calculation neither deletes stored bytes nor unlearns a trained model. It cannot discover unrecorded copies. The graph’s checkpoint-like node is fictional; this example has not trained a model.
What continues toward the decoder Only retained candidates continue to deduplication, final split construction and tokenization. The candidate set is kept in deterministic source and span order. Pending-review text cannot join it through a relabeled role or an incomplete output. A complete receipt preserves the selected policy, source references and counts. That makes the filtering decision reproducible, not universally correct. The scalar decoder remains unchanged, and this small example establishes neither real-corpus retention rates nor trained-model quality, privacy or memorization safety.

First-terminal decision The first rule that rejects a record or holds it for manual review. Evaluation stops there; later rules have no result for that record.
Known-source withdrawal List a source's recorded descendants once in a supplied lineage graph. This calculation does not erase data, find unknown copies or unlearn a trained model.
Manual review A withheld disposition distinct from rejection and retention. This example supplies no approval override, so pending-review text cannot continue as training input.
Normalization Here, replace CRLF pairs with LF and trim only space, tab, CR and LF at the edges. Case, internal spaces and other Unicode characters remain unchanged.
Occurrence identity A digest binding a selected raw source to one half-open payload byte span. Equal text at different positions has different identities; changing filter policy does not change the raw occurrence.
Record frame One raw payload delimited by the selected separator or final end-of-input boundary. Its byte span excludes the separator and includes its own line endings.
Stage population The records that actually reach one rule after surviving every earlier rule. This count is that rule's rate denominator, not necessarily the whole input count.

<h2 id="the-problem-verified-text-is-not-yet-training-input">The problem: verified text is not yet training input</h2>
<p>A matching checksum tells us which text we have, not whether every record should
enter a training corpus. A record may be malformed, too large for the processing
budget, or contain a literal marker that our chosen policy excludes. Some records
need review rather than an automatic yes or no.</p>
<p>Deleting every excluded record without keeping its reason loses useful evidence.
Reporting only the final retained count also hides which records each rule
actually examined. If an early rule stops a record, later rules cannot truthfully
report that the record passed or failed them.</p>
<p>The solution here is an ordered filter with three dispositions:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Retained:</strong> a candidate for the next data-processing stage, not a guarantee
of quality, privacy or permission.</li>
<li><strong>Rejected:</strong> excluded by an automatic rule.</li>
<li><strong>Manual review:</strong> withheld from downstream training input. This example has
no approval override.</li>
</ul>
<p>The first rule in the configured order that rejects a record or holds it for
manual review supplies that record’s first terminal decision. Evaluation stops
there; later rules are not evaluated for that record. If a record survives every
rule, it is retained with no first terminal rule. The report preserves each
record’s disposition, the rules actually evaluated, any first terminal rule and
the record’s reference to its raw source. It does not copy excluded text into
public findings.</p>
<h2 id="eight-records-with-explicit-boundaries">Eight records, with explicit boundaries</h2>
<p>Everything in the worked example is course-authored synthetic data. It is not a
filtering result for TinyStories. The two source names <code>fixture-train</code> and
<code>fixture-validation</code> preserve their raw-source provenance; they do not create
the final training, validation or test split.</p>
<p>The selected framing policy, <code>end-of-input-delimited-v2</code>, recognizes the ASCII
marker <code><|endoftext|></code> only when it occupies an entire physical line. A marker
line may end with LF, CRLF or end of input. Its bytes are a delimiter, not payload
text. The same marker inside an ordinary text line is not a delimiter.</p>
<p>End of input also closes a remaining nonempty payload, even without a final
newline. End of input immediately after a separator creates no extra record.
Consecutive separators create an empty payload that the filter can reject.
A failed read is an error, not an end-of-input boundary. These rules are selected
explicitly; the reader does not guess another format after a failure.</p>
<p>For this fixture, append <code>b"<|endoftext|>\n"</code> after every record below, in table
order within each source. Every separator therefore contributes <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>14</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">14</span></span></span></span> bytes.
In Rust literals, <code>\n</code> denotes one LF byte and <code>\xff</code> one byte that is invalid
as standalone UTF-8.</p>

<h2 id="the-solution-stop-once-count-at-every-reached-rule">The solution: stop once, count at every reached rule</h2>
<p>The fixture deliberately uses small thresholds so each failure is visible:</p>
<ol>
<li>Reject a raw payload above <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">64</span></span></span></span> bytes before decoding it.</li>
<li>Reject invalid UTF-8.</li>
<li>Normalize the decoded text and reject fewer than <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span> normalized UTF-8 bytes.</li>
<li>Reject fewer than <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span> ASCII letter.</li>
<li>Reject the literal <code>demo-key=CANARY</code>, matched without ASCII case distinctions.</li>
<li>Hold the literal <code>contact=</code>, matched case-sensitively.</li>
<li>Hold text below the configured ASCII-letter share.</li>
</ol>
<p>Normalization replaces CRLF pairs with LF, then trims only space, tab, CR and LF
at the two edges. It preserves case, internal spaces and other Unicode
characters. Length after normalization is measured in UTF-8 <strong>bytes</strong>, not
characters or tokens.</p>
<p>For the last rule, count Unicode scalar values other than the six ASCII
whitespace characters: space, tab, LF, vertical tab, form feed and CR. The
numerator counts ASCII letters among those values. Compare a configured
fraction using checked integer cross-products, rather than rounding a
floating-point ratio. A zero denominator is unavailable and sends a reached
record to review; it is not an observed share of zero. The fixture’s threshold
is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0/1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">0/1</span></span></span></span>, so its last survivor passes this rule.</p>
<p>These thresholds are not the full-corpus policy. The planned corpus policy uses
a <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>65,536</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65{,}536</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">65</span><span class="mord"><span class="mpunct">,</span></span><span class="mord">536</span></span></span></span>-byte raw limit, at least <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">16</span></span></span></span> normalized bytes, at least <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">8</span></span></span></span> ASCII
letters and an ASCII-letter share of at least <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">1/2</span></span></span></span>, with its own selected marker
lists. For example, the fixture’s short secret record would reach a different
first terminal rule under a stricter length threshold. None of the fixture’s
rates are measurements of a real corpus.</p>

</ul>
<p>Four records reach the secret-marker rule, and it rejects two. Its terminal
fraction is <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/4=1/2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">2/4</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">1/2</span></span></span></span>. Dividing by the original eight records gives <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/8=1/4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">2/8</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">1/4</span></span></span></span>,
a different quantity: that rule’s terminal decisions as a fraction of all input
records. Do not label the second quantity as the reached-population rate.</p>
<p>The reached populations are <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8,7,6,5,4,2,1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8389em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord">8</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">7</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">6</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">5</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">4</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span>, leaving one retained record.

<h2 id="rust-owns-the-framing-and-decisions">Rust owns the framing and decisions</h2>
<p>The framer accepts an ordinary <code>Read</code> source. The output interface separates
retained rows from body-free exclusion findings, without requiring a directory,
filename, HTTP source or storage backend. Supporting libraries provide JSON
encoding and SHA-256; the course code owns boundaries, rule order, terminal
decisions and accounting.</p>
<p>A bounded buffer retains only payloads within the selected size limit. An
oversized record is drained to its boundary and counted without retaining its
whole body. Read-buffer boundaries do not split records or invalidate a Unicode
character: UTF-8 decoding happens on the complete bounded payload.</p>

there; the manual-marker rule is <strong>not evaluated</strong> for that record. Swap those
two rules and <code>r7</code> is held for review instead. The new totals are one retained,
five rejected and two pending review. The same raw bytes therefore produce
different reasons and dispositions under different policies.</p>

<p>A quoted marker can cause a false positive. Sensitive text without a configured
literal can pass. Likewise, few ASCII letters do not prove that a record is bad
or that it is not English, and many ASCII letters do not establish language or
quality. These heuristics need corpus-specific inspection, including inspection
of excluded text under appropriate access controls.</p>

<p>A finding contains a source reference, half-open raw byte span, occurrence ID,
evaluated rule IDs and the terminal decision. It contains no excluded body,
snippet or matched capture. The occurrence ID binds the selected raw artifact,
source and payload IDs, raw file digest and span. Equal text at different spans
has different occurrence IDs. A changed filter policy does not change those raw
occurrence IDs, but does change the derived artifact’s policy identity.</p>
<p>Per source and terminal reason, the report includes the first <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">32</span></span></span></span> occurrence
IDs in input order as samples. The full finding stream and counters remain
complete: the sample bound is not permission to stop counting. Findings and
the receipt share a strict metadata budget below <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">100</span></span></span></span> MiB. Exceeding that
budget fails the attempt; it does not silently truncate evidence.</p>
<p>Byte accounting uses separate bases. Separator bytes are outside raw payload
spans. Payloads rejected before decoding still contribute to the raw total.
Normalized byte totals include only records actually decoded and normalized.
A complete run reads <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>287</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">287</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">287</span></span></span></span> physical bytes: <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>175</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">175</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">175</span></span></span></span> payload bytes and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>112</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">112</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">112</span></span></span></span>
delimiter bytes. Of the payload bytes, <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>68</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">68</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">68</span></span></span></span> belong to records rejected before
decoding and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>107</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">107</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">107</span></span></span></span> are decoded. Normalization leaves <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>101</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">101</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">101</span></span></span></span> bytes across decoded
records: <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">8</span></span></span></span> retained, <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>65</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">65</span></span></span></span> rejected and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>28</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">28</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">28</span></span></span></span> pending review. These are byte
counts, not token counts; excluded text still contributes to its applicable
accounting totals.</p>
<p>A retained row is checked again against the selected filtered artifact, policy,
source references, span and text digest before consumption. Relabeling a
manual-review payload or selecting an untrusted candidate’s own manifest does
not make it eligible.</p>

<p>The JSON report records eight inputs, one retained record, six rejected records
and one pending-review record, plus each rule’s reached count and terminal
fraction. Its changed-order comparison records one retained, five rejected
and two pending review. Artifact digests identify the actual policy and source
bytes; do not replace them with illustrative hashes.</p>

<h2 id="history-inspect-what-filtering-removes">History: inspect what filtering removes</h2>
<p>A binary keep/drop report hides the reason for exclusion and the population that
each later rule actually inspected.</p>
<p>The C4 study examines text removed by filters; RefinedWeb later combines
filtering and deduplication in a web-scale corpus.</p>
<p>Dodge and colleagues inspect C4 exclusions and find disproportionate removal of
content concerning minority groups by its word blocklist. Their 2021
<a href="https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.98/">Documenting Large Webtext Corpora: A Case Study on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus</a>
motivates examining removals rather than assuming that a filter is neutral.</p>
<p>Penedo and colleagues describe a large web corpus built with filtering and
deduplication, and evaluate language models trained on its data. Their 2023
<a href="https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/fa3ed726cc5073b9c31e3e49a807789c-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html">RefinedWeb paper</a>
concerns a much broader pipeline than this eight-record fixture. Its model
results do not certify our heuristics or isolate a benefit from one rule.</p>
<p>The Rust contrast below is course-local: it reduces our existing decisions to
one exclusion bit. It is not an implementation reproduced from either paper.
It counts seven excluded records but loses their rejection-versus-review
distinction and cannot say which later rule saw each one.</p>

<p>Record explicit exclusions and stage populations before deduplication and
training; a passed heuristic is not a quality, privacy or memorization guarantee.</p>

<p>The secret-marker rule’s denominator is its four reached records, not all eight
inputs. After its two terminal decisions, only two records reach the
manual-marker rule. One of those two is held for manual review; the other
survives the rule.
The diagram leaves <code>r7</code>’s later manual-marker result absent rather than inventing
a pass or fail for an operation that never occurred.</p>

<h2 id="optional-practice-inspect-the-recorded-evidence">Optional practice: inspect the recorded evidence</h2>
<h3 id="source-withdrawal-is-a-known-lineage-calculation">Source withdrawal is a known-lineage calculation</h3>
<p>Filtering also preserves source lineage so a later withdrawal can identify
recorded downstream artifacts. The separate fictional graph uses <code>r0</code> as a
<strong>raw-source node alias</strong>, not as the worked table’s record label or an actual
occurrence digest. Its descendants are <code>a0</code>, <code>f0</code>, <code>s0</code>, <code>tok0</code> and <code>w0</code>.
Two paths reach <code>w0</code>; the result lists it once. The unrelated branch <code>f9</code>
belongs to a different source and is not in this withdrawal’s descendant set.</p>

<details><summary>Checked explanations for the three reproduction tasks</summary><ol>
<li>
<p>The trailing LF byte in each decoded fixture payload remains part of the raw
payload and physical source byte counts, but normalization trims it from the
end of the decoded text. Internal LF characters remain unchanged. Trimming
the trailing LF changes the normalized byte count, not the number of bytes
read from the raw source.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>With the secret-marker rule first, <code>r7</code> is rejected and never reaches the
manual-marker rule. With the manual-marker rule first, <code>r7</code> is held for review
and never reaches the secret-marker rule.
The raw source and occurrence identities do not change. The derived policy
and artifact identities change because the ordered filtering policy is
different.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The descendant set contains <code>a0</code>, <code>f0</code>, <code>s0</code>, <code>tok0</code> and <code>w0</code>, with <code>w0</code>
listed once despite its two incoming paths; it excludes the unrelated <code>f9</code>.
This calculation neither deletes stored bytes nor unlearns a trained model.
It cannot discover unrecorded copies. The graph’s checkpoint-like node is
fictional; this example has not trained a model.</p>
</li>
</ol></details>

<h2 id="what-continues-toward-the-decoder">What continues toward the decoder</h2>
<p>Only retained candidates continue to deduplication, final split construction and
tokenization. The candidate set is kept in deterministic source and span order.
Pending-review text cannot join it through a relabeled role or an incomplete
output.</p>
<p>A complete receipt preserves the selected policy, source references and counts.
That makes the filtering decision reproducible, not universally correct. The
scalar decoder remains unchanged, and this small example establishes neither
real-corpus retention rates nor trained-model quality, privacy or memorization

<h2 id="the-problem-available-text-does-not-identify-a-training-corpus">The problem: available text does not identify a training corpus</h2>
<p>An LLM learns from the text supplied to its training pipeline. A filename alone
does not identify that text: two files named <code>train.txt</code> can contain different
bytes. A source can also change between revisions. Even the intended text is an
incomplete corpus record if its source revision, license text or attribution
has been lost.</p>
<p>Before filtering or tokenizing, we need to connect the selected text to its
documented origin and check that the supplied bytes match that selection. The
same check should work whether those bytes arrive from a file, an HTTP client
or another reader, and whether the verified bundle is kept in memory, files or
another store. How bytes travel and where they are kept do not change which
content was selected.</p>
<p>This chapter implements that content boundary. Verification does not clean the
text, establish privacy, grant legal permission or measure its usefulness for
training.</p>
<h2 id="start-with-a-complete-tiny-corpus-bundle">Start with a complete, tiny corpus bundle</h2>
<p>The example uses course-authored test bytes, not a downloaded training dataset.
A <strong>payload</strong> is one byte sequence included in the bundle. A <strong>content ID</strong> is
its logical name within the selected record, not a filename or a URL.</p>

<h2 id="the-solution-select-the-record-then-verify-its-content">The solution: select the record, then verify its content</h2>
<p>A <strong>manifest</strong> records the bundle. Each payload entry supplies a content ID,
role, media type, exact byte count and SHA-256 digest. Each source record names
the corresponding content ID, source revision, provenance reference, license
and attribution. The provenance reference is descriptive evidence; it need not
be a URL and is not an instruction to fetch anything.</p>
<p>The caller must select the expected record independently of the candidate
being checked. Rust’s <code>DatasetPolicy</code> stores that selection. Copying an
untrusted candidate into the expected policy would check only its internal
consistency, not whether it was the intended corpus. The verifier cannot make
the caller’s provenance claims true merely by matching them.</p>
<p>For this tiny example, the selected record contains <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> sources and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span> payloads.
The reusable verifier does not require those counts. Other selections can name
different numbers of sources, share metadata or include additional payloads.</p>
<p>The manifest has one <strong>canonical</strong> representation: compact UTF-8 JSON, object
keys sorted by their UTF-8 bytes, payload entries sorted by the UTF-8 bytes of
their content IDs, source entries sorted by the UTF-8 bytes of their source IDs,
and exactly one final newline. An incoming manifest
with different formatting or ordering is rejected, not silently rewritten.
This fixes the exact bytes used for identity:</p>

including payload digests and provenance. <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">SHA256</mi><mo>⁡</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{SHA256}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mop"><span class="mord mathrm">SHA256</span></span></span></span></span> maps those

<h2 id="verify-supplied-bytes-without-choosing-their-transport">Verify supplied bytes without choosing their transport</h2>
<p>The content verifier performs three checks in order:</p>
<ol>
<li>Validate the candidate manifest’s structure and require exact agreement with
the independently selected policy, including its provenance and producer
identifiers.</li>
<li>Require the provider’s logical inventory to match the selected payload IDs
exactly. A missing, extra or duplicate ID causes refusal before payloads are
opened or destination staging is created.</li>
<li>Read every selected payload through standard Rust I/O. Compare its observed
length and digest with its selected entry. Accept the bundle only after every
payload passes.</li>
</ol>
<p><code>AssetSource</code> supplies the logical inventory and a standard <code>Read</code> reader for
each selected payload. The provider decides how to obtain those bytes. Filesystem
path safety and HTTP response handling belong to the relevant adapter or library,
not to the content checks. A future provider can implement the same interface
without adding a new retrieval mode to the verifier.</p>
<p><code>verify_payload_into</code> uses standard I/O to stream into a writer while the
course code counts bytes and updates the digest. For a selected <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span>-byte payload,
it observes at most <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span> bytes: the fourth distinguishes a complete <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span>-byte stream
from a longer stream with the same prefix. That excess byte is not written to
the destination. A short stream fails with <code>Size</code>; so does an overrun.
Equal-length content with the wrong digest fails with <code>Hash</code>. A reader or
writer failure is <code>Io</code>, not successful end of input.</p>

<p>SHA-256 and JSON syntax use supporting libraries. Course Rust owns record
consistency, canonical ordering, selected-policy agreement, logical inventory
and the comparisons that decide admission.</p>
<h3 id="keep-incomplete-content-out-of-the-published-bundle">Keep incomplete content out of the published bundle</h3>
<p><code>AssetStore</code> creates a private stage with standard <code>Write</code> writers.
A writer may contain an unverified prefix when verification fails. Such bytes
must remain unpublished; the caller must not treat them as an admitted payload.</p>
<p><code>acquire_bundle</code> verifies each payload, finishes it in the private stage,
and calls <code>publish</code> only after the entire bundle passes. The storage adapter
owns atomic publication, durability and cleanup. The content algorithm does not
assume a directory layout, reserved manifest filename or database protocol.</p>
<p>The example uses a memory store. Its failed replacement leaves the prior bundle
unchanged and publishes no partial candidate. This demonstrates the admission
order and this store’s behavior, not crash durability for every possible storage
backend. An adapter must publish a complete bundle or none of it; a storage error
after publication may leave a complete bundle visible and must not be described
as proof of rollback.</p>

<h3 id="two-changes-that-expose-the-boundary">Two changes that expose the boundary</h3>
<p>Replacing <code>b"abc"</code> with <code>b"abd"</code> preserves the training payload’s <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span>-byte
length. A byte-count check accepts the replacement, but the full verifier returns
<code>Hash</code>. This identifies a content mismatch, not what either text would teach
an LLM.</p>
<p>For a separate deliberate selection, change attribution to
<code>b"course-authored fixture v2\n"</code>. Its payload entry now records <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>27</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">27</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">27</span></span></span></span> bytes and
a different digest. The source records still refer to the same logical
attribution ID; the raw text digests remain unchanged. The new complete payload
totals <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>49</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">49</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">49</span></span></span></span> bytes, and its canonical manifest has a different identity.
The original policy refuses this variant until the caller independently selects
the new record; changing supplied metadata does not authorize itself.</p>
<p><code>replay_bundle</code> reads a canonical manifest, checks the selected artifact
identity and verifies every currently supplied payload again. It has no
destination-writing interface. Matching an old identity alone would not detect
payload bytes changed afterward.</p>
<p>The executable prints a report with scope <code>synthetic-offline-fixture</code>,
including all payload counts and digests, the attribution comparison,
complete replay and the preserved prior bundle. These are checked toy results,
not acquisition of a training dataset.</p>

<p>Run the demo from the repository root, the directory containing <code>course</code>,
with Docker installed and running. Set <code>COURSE_CORPUS=false</code> because this example
uses only its tiny built-in inputs, not the optional large corpus. If the workspace
image is absent, the wrapper first builds it using network access for dependencies;
the demo itself then runs with network access disabled:</p>
<pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6;overflow-x:auto" tabindex="0" data-language="sh" dir="ltr"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">COURSE_CORPUS</span><span style="color:#FF9492">=</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF">false</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> ./course</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> run</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> cargo</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> run</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --offline</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> --locked</span><span style="color:#91CBFF"> -p</span><span style="color:#ADDCFF"> ch41-governed-corpus-acquisition</span></span></code></pre>

<h2 id="history-preserve-dataset-context-beside-the-bytes">History: preserve dataset context beside the bytes</h2>
<p>A byte-count inventory detects missing or truncated content, but equal-length
<code>abc</code> and <code>abd</code> expose its limit. The following Rust function demonstrates
that narrow baseline; it does not reenact a historical dataset project’s full
process.</p>
<figure class="rust-source" data-source-path="rust/demos/ch41-governed-corpus-acquisition/src/lib.rs" data-source-region="size-only-contrast" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5> <figcaption data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5> <span data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5>The course-local byte-count baseline accepts both three-byte inputs, abc and abd; it does not establish content identity or provenance.</span> <code dir="ltr" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5>rust/demos/ch41-governed-corpus-acquisition/src/lib.rs#size-only-contrast</code> </figcaption> <pre class="astro-code github-dark-high-contrast rust-source-code" style="background-color:#0a0c10;color:#f0f3f6; overflow-x: auto;" tabindex="0" aria-label="Rust source: the limited corpus byte-count baseline" dir="ltr" data-astro-cid-i3uagjh5 data-language="rust"><code><span class="line"><span style="color:#FF9492">pub</span><span style="color:#FF9492"> fn</span><span style="color:#DBB7FF"> size_only_accepts</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">(expected_bytes</span><span style="color:#FF9492">:</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> u64</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">, supplied</span><span style="color:#FF9492">:</span><span style="color:#FF9492"> &</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">[</span><span style="color:#FFB757">u8</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">]) </span><span style="color:#FF9492">-></span><span style="color:#FFB757"> bool</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6"> {</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">    supplied</span><span style="color:#FF9492">.</span><span style="color:#DBB7FF">len</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6">() </span><span style="color:#FF9492">as</span><span style="color:#FFB757"> u64</span><span style="color:#FF9492"> ==</span><span style="color:#F0F3F6"> expected_bytes</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="color:#F0F3F6">}</span></span></code></pre> </figure>
<p>A byte inventory alone does not preserve a dataset’s collection context,
provenance or suitability for language-model training.
Datasheets for Datasets proposes structured dataset documentation; the later
ROOTS corpus describes data creation, curation and governance for a multilingual
language-model corpus.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010v8">Datasheets for Datasets</a>, first posted in
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2018</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2018</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2018</span></span></span></span> and revised in the linked <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2021</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2021</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2021</span></span></span></span> version, provides the earlier example.
Gebru and colleagues propose dataset documentation describing motivation,
composition, collection and recommended uses to improve communication,
transparency and accountability. A checksum cannot replace those informed
judgments.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03915v1">The BigScience ROOTS Corpus</a> is described
in a <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2023</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2023</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2023</span></span></span></span> preprint. The ROOTS corpus paper documents data creation and curation
with governance foregrounded in a multilingual language-model project; it does
not validate this chapter’s fixture. The tiny manifest is not the ROOTS
governance process or proof of corpus suitability.</p>
<p>Keep selected corpus bytes linked to their source context before downstream
filtering, split construction and training. Byte agreement does not establish
quality, privacy or permission. Documentation records context; byte verification
checks agreement with a selection. Neither alone establishes privacy, permission
or training quality.</p>

<h2 id="read-the-evidence-directly">Read the evidence directly</h2>
<p>A spatial diagram would not clarify these record comparisons. The payload table
states exactly which bytes belong to each role; the Rust report records identity
changes, digest refusal and complete replay directly. Together they distinguish
the selected corpus record, its supplied bytes and the synthetic scope of the
example.</p>

<details><summary>Checked explanations for the three corpus-content verification tasks</summary><ol>
<li>Both <code>abc</code> and <code>abd</code> contain <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3</span></span></span></span> bytes, but their digests differ.

their original digests. The changed canonical manifest changes the identity.
The variant needs its own independently selected policy.</li>
<li>The test injects a corrupt final payload and separate write, finish and
publication failures. In each case the memory store keeps the prior bundle
and publishes no replacement. Earlier verified payloads remain in private
staging, not in a partially admitted bundle. This is the tested memory-store
boundary, not a guarantee of crash recovery for arbitrary storage.</li>

ordinary Read input and bounded framing to independently selected complete-source length/digest verification and provisional-output refusal; explain normalization and first-terminal filtering, the absent later result for r7, swapped dispositions and the limits of the two literal-marker heuristics.","value":"Rust owns the framing and decisions The framer accepts an ordinary Read source. The output interface separates retained rows from body-free exclusion findings, without requiring a directory, filename, HTTP source or storage backend. Supporting libraries provide JSON encoding and SHA-256; the course code owns boundaries, rule order, terminal decisions and accounting. A bounded buffer retains only payloads within the selected size limit. An oversized record is drained to its boundary and counted without retaining its whole body. Read-buffer boundaries do not split records or invalidate a Unicode character: UTF-8 decoding happens on the complete bounded payload. Read the selected raw source completely and check its byte count and digest after framing. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/stream.rs#source-bound-framing pub fn scan_source<R: Read, F>( reader: R, source: &SourceBinding, policy: &FramingPolicy, mut visit: F, ) -> Result<ScanSummary, DataError> where F: FnMut(Frame) -> Result<(), DataError>, { policy.validate()?; let limit = source.bytes().checked_add(1).ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; let mut reader = reader.take(limit); let mut buffer = [0_u8; STREAM_BUFFER_BYTES]; let mut hasher = Sha256::new(); let mut observed = 0_u64; let mut framer = Framer::new(policy)?; loop { let length = reader.read(&mut buffer)?; if length == 0 { break; } observed = observed .checked_add(length as u64) .ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; if observed > source.bytes() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } hasher.update(&buffer[..length]); for &byte in &buffer[..length] { framer.feed(byte, &mut visit)?; } } framer.finish(&mut visit)?; if observed != source.bytes() || format!("{:x}", hasher.finalize()) != source.file_sha256() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } Ok(framer.summary) } The raw source was selected independently before this read. A report succeeds only after the complete source’s observed length and digest agree with that selection. Rows emitted before that final check are provisional. reading.roleRequirement: Explain why byte-verified text still needs record admission; explain how losing exclusion reasons and reporting only final totals hide actual rule populations; establish retained, rejected and withheld manual-review dispositions. State that the first reached rejecting or review rule supplies a terminal decision and stops evaluation, while surviving every rule yields retention with no first terminal rule; do not imply quality, privacy or permission approval.
reading.value: The problem: verified text is not yet training input A matching checksum tells us which text we have, not whether every record should enter a training corpus. A record may be malformed, too large for the processing budget, or contain a literal marker that our chosen policy excludes. Some records need review rather than an automatic yes or no. Deleting every excluded record without keeping its reason loses useful evidence. Reporting only the final retained count also hides which records each rule actually examined. If an early rule stops a record, later rules cannot truthfully report that the record passed or failed them. The solution here is an ordered filter with three dispositions: Retained: a candidate for the next data-processing stage, not a guarantee of quality, privacy or permission. Rejected: excluded by an automatic rule. Manual review: withheld from downstream training input. This example has no approval override. The first rule in the configured order that rejects a record or holds it for manual review supplies that record’s first terminal decision. Evaluation stops there; later rules are not evaluated for that record. If a record survives every rule, it is retained with no first terminal rule. The report preserves each record’s disposition, the rules actually evaluated, any first terminal rule and the record’s reference to its raw source. It does not copy excluded text into public findings.

Eight records, with explicit boundaries Everything in the worked example is course-authored synthetic data. It is not a filtering result for TinyStories. The two source names fixture-train and fixture-validation preserve their raw-source provenance; they do not create the final training, validation or test split. The selected framing policy, end-of-input-delimited-v2, recognizes the ASCII marker <|endoftext|> only when it occupies an entire physical line. A marker line may end with LF, CRLF or end of input. Its bytes are a delimiter, not payload text. The same marker inside an ordinary text line is not a delimiter. End of input also closes a remaining nonempty payload, even without a final newline. End of input immediately after a separator creates no extra record. Consecutive separators create an empty payload that the filter can reject. A failed read is an error, not an end-of-input boundary. These rules are selected explicitly; the reader does not guess another format after a failure. For this fixture, append b"<|endoftext|>
" after every record below, in table order within each source. Every separator therefore contributes 14 bytes. In Rust literals,

" | 9 | None; retained r1 | fixture-train | b"\xff
" | 2 | Strict UTF-8; rejected r2 | fixture-train | 65 copies of b'x', then b"
" | 66 | Raw size; rejected r3 | fixture-train | b"hi
