reading.value: The solution: stop once, count at every reached rule The fixture deliberately uses small thresholds so each failure is visible: Reject a raw payload above 64 bytes before decoding it. Reject invalid UTF-8. Normalize the decoded text and reject fewer than 4 normalized UTF-8 bytes. Reject fewer than 1 ASCII letter. Reject the literal demo-key=CANARY, matched without ASCII case distinctions. Hold the literal contact=, matched case-sensitively. Hold text below the configured ASCII-letter share. Normalization replaces CRLF pairs with LF, then trims only space, tab, CR and LF at the two edges. It preserves case, internal spaces and other Unicode characters. Length after normalization is measured in UTF-8 bytes, not characters or tokens. For the last rule, count Unicode scalar values other than the six ASCII whitespace characters: space, tab, LF, vertical tab, form feed and CR. The numerator counts ASCII letters among those values. Compare a configured fraction using checked integer cross-products, rather than rounding a floating-point ratio. A zero denominator is unavailable and sends a reached record to review; it is not an observed share of zero. The fixture’s threshold is 0/1, so its last survivor passes this rule. These thresholds are not the full-corpus policy. The planned corpus policy uses a 65{,}536-byte raw limit, at least 16 normalized bytes, at least 8 ASCII letters and an ASCII-letter share of at least 1/2, with its own selected marker lists. For example, the fixture’s short secret record would reach a different first terminal rule under a stricter length threshold. None of the fixture’s rates are measurements of a real corpus. For a named rule k, report its terminal fraction using the population that actually reached it: r_k=\frac{n_{\mathrm{disposition},k}}{n_{\mathrm{seen},k}}

reading.roleRequirement: Define every symbol in the terminal fraction, its dimensionless unit and unavailable zero-input state; explain two terminal decisions among four reached records versus among eight originals; relate shrinking stage populations and the retained/rejected/manual-review count conservation without merging review into rejection.
reading.value: Symbols in the filtering fraction k identifies a rule in the configured order. n_{\mathrm{seen},k} counts records surviving every earlier rule and reaching rule k. n_{\mathrm{disposition},k} counts reached records whose first terminal decision is rejection or a hold for review at rule k. r_k is dimensionless. When n_{\mathrm{seen},k}=0, the report stores unavailable, not zero. Four records reach the secret-marker rule, and it rejects two. Its terminal fraction is 2/4=1/2. Dividing by the original eight records gives 2/8=1/4, a different quantity: that rule’s terminal decisions as a fraction of all input records. Do not label the second quantity as the reached-population rate. The reached populations are 8,7,6,5,4,2,1, leaving one retained record. The final dispositions must conserve the input count: 8=1_{\mathrm{retained}}+6_{\mathrm{rejected}}+1_{\mathrm{manual\ review}} A binary exclusion summary gives 7 ineligible records, but those are 6 rejections plus 1 pending review. Calling all seven “rejected” discards the distinction needed to explain their outcomes.

reading.roleRequirement: Connect ordinary Read input and bounded framing to independently selected complete-source length/digest verification and provisional-output refusal; explain normalization and first-terminal filtering, the absent later result for r7, swapped dispositions and the limits of the two literal-marker heuristics.
reading.value:
Rust owns the framing and decisions The framer accepts an ordinary Read source. The output interface separates retained rows from body-free exclusion findings, without requiring a directory, filename, HTTP source or storage backend. Supporting libraries provide JSON encoding and SHA-256; the course code owns boundaries, rule order, terminal decisions and accounting. A bounded buffer retains only payloads within the selected size limit. An oversized record is drained to its boundary and counted without retaining its whole body. Read-buffer boundaries do not split records or invalidate a Unicode character: UTF-8 decoding happens on the complete bounded payload. Read the selected raw source completely and check its byte count and digest after framing. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/stream.rs#source-bound-framing pub fn scan_source<R: Read, F>( reader: R, source: &SourceBinding, policy: &FramingPolicy, mut visit: F, ) -> Result<ScanSummary, DataError> where F: FnMut(Frame) -> Result<(), DataError>, { policy.validate()?; let limit = source.bytes().checked_add(1).ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; let mut reader = reader.take(limit); let mut buffer = [0_u8; STREAM_BUFFER_BYTES]; let mut hasher = Sha256::new(); let mut observed = 0_u64; let mut framer = Framer::new(policy)?; loop { let length = reader.read(&mut buffer)?; if length == 0 { break; } observed = observed .checked_add(length as u64) .ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; if observed > source.bytes() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } hasher.update(&buffer[..length]); for &byte in &buffer[..length] { framer.feed(byte, &mut visit)?; } } framer.finish(&mut visit)?; if observed != source.bytes() || format!("{:x}", hasher.finalize()) != source.file_sha256() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } Ok(framer.summary) } The raw source was selected independently before this read. A report succeeds only after the complete source’s observed length and digest agree with that selection. Rows emitted before that final check are provisional. A changed byte, truncated read or I/O error prevents publication of the completed result; a prefix must not become training input. Replace each CRLF pair with LF, then trim only space, tab, CR and LF from both text edges; preserve the remaining text. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/filter.rs#narrow-normalization pub fn normalize(text: &str) -> String { text.replace("
", "
") .trim_matches([' ', '	', '', '
']) .to_owned() } For one record, evaluate the configured rules in order and stop at its first rejection or manual-review decision. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/filter.rs#ordered-record-filter pub fn evaluate(frame: &Frame, policy: &FilterPolicy) -> Result<Decision, DataError> { policy.validate()?; let raw_bytes = frame.raw_bytes()?; let mut visited = vec![Rule::RawSize]; if raw_bytes > policy.framing.max_payload_bytes { return Ok(Decision::terminal(raw_bytes, visited, Rule::RawSize, None)); } let bytes = match &frame.data { FrameData::Bytes(bytes) if bytes.len() as u64 == raw_bytes => bytes, _ => return Err(DataError::InvalidRecord("frame body/span disagreement")), }; visited.push(Rule::Utf8); let text = match std::str::from_utf8(bytes) { Ok(text) => normalize(text), Err(_) => return Ok(Decision::terminal(raw_bytes, visited, Rule::Utf8, None)), }; let normalized_bytes = text.len() as u64; for &rule in &policy.stages[2..] { visited.push(rule); if normalized_terminal(&text, rule, policy)? { return Ok(Decision::terminal( raw_bytes, visited, rule, Some(normalized_bytes), )); } } Ok(Decision { disposition: Disposition::Retained, evaluated_rules: visited, first_terminal_rule: None, normalized_bytes: Some(normalized_bytes), raw_decoded: true, raw_bytes, retained_text: Some(text), }) } Record r7 contains both markers. With the secret rule first, it is rejected there; the manual-marker rule is not evaluated for that record. Swap those two rules and r7 is held for review instead. The new totals are one retained, five rejected and two pending review. The same raw bytes therefore produce different reasons and dispositions under different policies. Match secret-marker literals without ASCII case distinctions and manual-review literals case-sensitively; neither rule detects all sensitive text. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/privacy.rs#literal-marker-decisions pub fn contains_ascii_case_insensitive(text: &str, markers: &[String]) -> bool { markers.iter().any(|marker| { !marker.is_empty() && text .as_bytes() .windows(marker.len()) .any(|window| window.eq_ignore_ascii_case(marker.as_bytes())) }) } pub fn contains_case_sensitive(text: &str, markers: &[String]) -> bool { markers .iter() .any(|marker| !marker.is_empty() && text.contains(marker)) } A quoted marker can cause a false positive. Sensitive text without a configured literal can pass. Likewise, few ASCII letters do not prove that a record is bad or that it is not English, and many ASCII letters do not establish language or quality. These heuristics need corpus-specific inspection, including inspection of excluded text under appropriate access controls.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain body-free findings, raw occurrence versus derived policy/artifact identity, bounded samples versus complete counters and metadata-budget refusal; distinguish physical, payload, delimiter, decoded and normalized byte totals; require independently selected retained eligibility and provide the synthetic demo command, setup and observable report.
reading.value: Preserve counts without exposing excluded bodies Increment a rule's seen count only when the record reaches it, then count survival or its first terminal decision. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/governance.rs#stage-accounting fn record(&mut self, decision: &Decision, record_id: &str) -> Result<(), DataError> { for &rule in &decision.evaluated_rules { let stage = self .stages .iter_mut() .find(|stage| stage.rule == rule) .ok_or(DataError::InvalidRecord("unknown evaluated stage"))?; add(&mut stage.seen, 1)?; if decision.first_terminal_rule == Some(rule) { add(&mut stage.terminal, 1)?; } else { add(&mut stage.survived, 1)?; } } if decision.raw_decoded { add(&mut self.decoded_raw_bytes, decision.raw_bytes)?; } else { add(&mut self.undecoded_raw_bytes, decision.raw_bytes)?; } let normalized = decision.normalized_bytes.unwrap_or(0); add(&mut self.normalized_bytes, normalized)?; match decision.disposition { Disposition::Retained => { add(&mut self.retained, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_retained_bytes, normalized)?; } Disposition::Rejected => { add(&mut self.rejected, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_rejected_bytes, normalized)?; } Disposition::ManualReview => { add(&mut self.manual_review, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_manual_bytes, normalized)?; } } let sample = self .samples .iter_mut() .find(|group| { group.disposition == decision.disposition && group.first_terminal_rule == decision.first_terminal_rule }) .ok_or(DataError::InvalidRecord("sample group"))?; if sample.record_ids.len() < SAMPLE_REFERENCES_PER_GROUP { sample.record_ids.push(record_id.to_owned()); } Ok(()) } A finding contains a source reference, half-open raw byte span, occurrence ID, evaluated rule IDs and the terminal decision. It contains no excluded body, snippet or matched capture. The occurrence ID binds the selected raw artifact, source and payload IDs, raw file digest and span. Equal text at different spans has different occurrence IDs. A changed filter policy does not change those raw occurrence IDs, but does change the derived artifact’s policy identity. Per source and terminal reason, the report includes the first 32 occurrence IDs in input order as samples. The full finding stream and counters remain complete: the sample bound is not permission to stop counting. Findings and the receipt share a strict metadata budget below 100 MiB. Exceeding that budget fails the attempt; it does not silently truncate evidence. Byte accounting uses separate bases. Separator bytes are outside raw payload spans. Payloads rejected before decoding still contribute to the raw total. Normalized byte totals include only records actually decoded and normalized. A complete run reads 287 physical bytes: 175 payload bytes and 112 delimiter bytes. Of the payload bytes, 68 belong to records rejected before decoding and 107 are decoded. Normalization leaves 101 bytes across decoded records: 8 retained, 65 rejected and 28 pending review. These are byte counts, not token counts; excluded text still contributes to its applicable accounting totals. A retained row is checked again against the selected filtered artifact, policy, source references, span and text digest before consumption. Relabeling a manual-review payload or selecting an untrusted candidate’s own manifest does not make it eligible. Run the offline synthetic fixture and print the report derived from the Rust decisions. rust/demos/ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering/src/main.rs#offline-filtering-example fn main() { match ch42_deterministic_corpus_filtering::demo_report().and_then(|report| { serde_json::to_string_pretty(&report).map_err(|_| { llm_from_scratch::functional::data::stream::DataError::InvalidRecord( "report serialization", ) }) }) { Ok(report) => println!("{report}"), Err(error) => { eprintln!("filter fixture failed: {error}"); std::process::exit(1); } } } To reproduce the example, start at the repository root with Docker installed and the course development image available. This command uses only synthetic bytes, so the corpus download is disabled: COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering The JSON report records eight inputs, one retained record, six rejected records and one pending-review record, plus each rule’s reached count and terminal fraction. Its changed-order comparison records one retained, five rejected and two pending review. Artifact digests identify the actual policy and source bytes; do not replace them with illustrative hashes.

reading.roleRequirement: State the bounded C4 exclusion and RefinedWeb filtering/deduplication claims with their primary citations; distinguish aggregate corpus/model evidence from this fixture and identify the binary exclusion code as a course-local loss-of-information contrast, not a reproduction of either paper or a quality/privacy guarantee.
reading.value: History: inspect what filtering removes A binary keep/drop report hides the reason for exclusion and the population that each later rule actually inspected. The C4 study examines text removed by filters; RefinedWeb later combines filtering and deduplication in a web-scale corpus. Dodge and colleagues inspect C4 exclusions and find disproportionate removal of content concerning minority groups by its word blocklist. Their 2021 Documenting Large Webtext Corpora: A Case Study on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus motivates examining removals rather than assuming that a filter is neutral. Penedo and colleagues describe a large web corpus built with filtering and deduplication, and evaluate language models trained on its data. Their 2023 RefinedWeb paper concerns a much broader pipeline than this eight-record fixture. Its model results do not certify our heuristics or isolate a benefit from one rule. The Rust contrast below is course-local: it reduces our existing decisions to one exclusion bit. It is not an implementation reproduced from either paper. It counts seven excluded records but loses their rejection-versus-review distinction and cannot say which later rule saw each one. Reduce the fixture's three dispositions to one exclusion bit and expose the information that summary omits. rust/demos/ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering/src/lib.rs#binary-filter-contrast /// A course-local reporting contrast, not either paper's implementation. pub fn binary_exclusion(disposition: Disposition) -> bool { disposition != Disposition::Retained } Record explicit exclusions and stage populations before deduplication and training; a passed heuristic is not a quality, privacy or memorization guarantee.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain the figure's shrinking reached populations and r7's early terminal stop; identify the secret rule's four-record denominator and two terminal outcomes, the subsequent two records reaching the manual-marker rule, and its one held record and one survivor. Do not confuse reaching a rule with receiving manual review or invent a result for an unevaluated rule.
reading.value: See the shrinking population First-terminal filtering of eight synthetic records Each rule sees only survivors of earlier rules. The secret-marker rule rejects two of its four inputs; record r7 stops there, so the later manual-marker rule is not evaluated for that record. Reached populations in the synthetic fixture Rule Seen records Terminal records Surviving records Terminal fraction of seen Terminal outcome Raw payload limit 8 1 7 \frac{1}{8} Reject Strict UTF-8 7 1 6 \frac{1}{7} Reject Normalized byte minimum 6 1 5 \frac{1}{6} Reject ASCII letter minimum 5 1 4 \frac{1}{5} Reject Secret marker 4 2 2 \frac{2}{4} Reject Manual-review marker 2 1 1 \frac{1}{2} Hold for manual review ASCII-share review 1 0 1 \frac{0}{1} Hold for manual review Final dispositions in the synthetic fixture Retained records 1 Rejected records 6 Pending-review records 1 Record r7 stops at its first terminal rule First terminal rule for r7 Secret marker Later manual-marker evaluation for r7 Not evaluated Pending-review text stays withheld; the fixture provides no release override. The secret-marker rule’s denominator is its four reached records, not all eight inputs. After its two terminal decisions, only two records reach the manual-marker rule. One of those two is held for manual review; the other survives the rule. The diagram leaves r7’s later manual-marker result absent rather than inventing a pass or fail for an operation that never occurred.

reading.roleRequirement: Explain the fictional known-source lineage and once-only descendant result with its alias and non-erasure limits; offer three optional reproduction/inspection tasks with actual shared setup, exact commands and expected one selected passing test, followed by substantive matched explanations for trailing-LF edge trimming versus fixed raw counts and preserved internal LF, policy order/identity and known descendants.
reading.value: Optional practice: inspect the recorded evidence Source withdrawal is a known-lineage calculation Filtering also preserves source lineage so a later withdrawal can identify recorded downstream artifacts. The separate fictional graph uses r0 as a raw-source node alias, not as the worked table’s record label or an actual occurrence digest. Its descendants are a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0. Two paths reach w0; the result lists it once. The unrelated branch f9 belongs to a different source and is not in this withdrawal’s descendant set. Validate the supplied lineage graph, then list each known descendant of the selected raw source once; this does not erase stored data. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/deletion.rs#known-descendant-withdrawal pub fn withdrawal( &self, raw_roots: &[String], limits: GraphLimits, ) -> Result<WithdrawalPlan, DataError> { let kinds = self.validate(limits)?; let mut reached = BTreeSet::new(); let mut pending = BTreeSet::new(); for root in raw_roots { if kinds.get(root.as_str()) != Some(&NodeKind::RawSource) { return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown or non-source root")); } pending.insert(root.as_str()); } while let Some(id) = pending.pop_first() { if !reached.insert(id) { continue; } for edge in &self.edges { if edge.parent == id && !reached.contains(edge.child.as_str()) { pending.insert(edge.child.as_str()); } } } let mut artifacts = Vec::new(); let mut sources = Vec::new(); for id in reached { match kinds.get(id) { Some(NodeKind::RawSource) => sources.push(id.into()), Some(NodeKind::Artifact) => artifacts.push(id.into()), None => return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown reached node")), } } Ok(WithdrawalPlan { artifacts, sources }) } Run these commands from the repository root with Docker installed and running. Each selects exactly one test; expect one passing test, not zero selected tests. Reproduce the fixture’s byte accounting. Inspect the assertions linking payload, delimiter, decoded and normalized byte totals. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering fixture_counts_and_byte_conservation -- --exact Reproduce the comparison that places the manual-marker rule before the secret-marker rule. Inspect the first terminal decision for r7 and the identities compared by the test. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering swapping_secret_and_review_changes_first_terminal -- --exact Reproduce the known-lineage withdrawal. Inspect the assertions checking the sorted, duplicate-free descendant set. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering withdrawal_reaches_known_descendants_once -- --exact Checked explanations for the three reproduction tasks The trailing LF byte in each decoded fixture payload remains part of the raw payload and physical source byte counts, but normalization trims it from the end of the decoded text. Internal LF characters remain unchanged. Trimming the trailing LF changes the normalized byte count, not the number of bytes read from the raw source. With the secret-marker rule first, r7 is rejected and never reaches the manual-marker rule. With the manual-marker rule first, r7 is held for review and never reaches the secret-marker rule. The raw source and occurrence identities do not change. The derived policy and artifact identities change because the ordered filtering policy is different. The descendant set contains a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0, with w0 listed once despite its two incoming paths; it excludes the unrelated f9. This calculation neither deletes stored bytes nor unlearns a trained model. It cannot discover unrecorded copies. The graph’s checkpoint-like node is fictional; this example has not trained a model.

reading.value: What continues toward the decoder Only retained candidates continue to deduplication, final split construction and tokenization. The candidate set is kept in deterministic source and span order. Pending-review text cannot join it through a relabeled role or an incomplete output. A complete receipt preserves the selected policy, source references and counts. That makes the filtering decision reproducible, not universally correct. The scalar decoder remains unchanged, and this small example establishes neither real-corpus retention rates nor trained-model quality, privacy or memorization safety.

## The problem: verified text is not yet training input

A matching checksum tells us which text we have, not whether every record should
enter a training corpus. A record may be malformed, too large for the processing
budget, or contain a literal marker that our chosen policy excludes. Some records
need review rather than an automatic yes or no.

Deleting every excluded record without keeping its reason loses useful evidence.
Reporting only the final retained count also hides which records each rule
actually examined. If an early rule stops a record, later rules cannot truthfully
report that the record passed or failed them.

The solution here is an ordered filter with three dispositions:

- **Retained:** a candidate for the next data-processing stage, not a guarantee
  of quality, privacy or permission.
- **Rejected:** excluded by an automatic rule.
- **Manual review:** withheld from downstream training input. This example has
  no approval override.

The first rule in the configured order that rejects a record or holds it for
manual review supplies that record's first terminal decision. Evaluation stops
there; later rules are not evaluated for that record. If a record survives every
rule, it is retained with no first terminal rule. The report preserves each
record's disposition, the rules actually evaluated, any first terminal rule and
the record's reference to its raw source. It does not copy excluded text into
public findings.

## Eight records, with explicit boundaries

Everything in the worked example is course-authored synthetic data. It is not a
filtering result for TinyStories. The two source names `fixture-train` and
`fixture-validation` preserve their raw-source provenance; they do not create
the final training, validation or test split.

The selected framing policy, `end-of-input-delimited-v2`, recognizes the ASCII
marker `<|endoftext|>` only when it occupies an entire physical line. A marker
line may end with LF, CRLF or end of input. Its bytes are a delimiter, not payload
text. The same marker inside an ordinary text line is not a delimiter.

End of input also closes a remaining nonempty payload, even without a final
newline. End of input immediately after a separator creates no extra record.
Consecutive separators create an empty payload that the filter can reject.
A failed read is an error, not an end-of-input boundary. These rules are selected
explicitly; the reader does not guess another format after a failure.

For this fixture, append `b"<|endoftext|>\n"` after every record below, in table
order within each source. Every separator therefore contributes $14$ bytes.
In Rust literals, `\n` denotes one LF byte and `\xff` one byte that is invalid
as standalone UTF-8.

| Label | Source | Complete raw payload construction | Payload bytes | First terminal decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `r0` | `fixture-train` | `b"cat sat.\n"` | $9$ | None; retained |
| `r1` | `fixture-train` | `b"\xff\n"` | $2$ | Strict UTF-8; rejected |
| `r2` | `fixture-train` | $65$ copies of `b'x'`, then `b"\n"` | $66$ | Raw size; rejected |
| `r3` | `fixture-train` | `b"hi\n"` | $3$ | Minimum normalized length; rejected |
| `r4` | `fixture-validation` | `b"....\n"` | $5$ | Minimum ASCII letters; rejected |
| `r5` | `fixture-validation` | `b"demo-key=CANARY\n"` | $16$ | Secret marker; rejected |
| `r6` | `fixture-validation` | `b"contact=alex@example.invalid\n"` | $29$ | Manual marker; held |
| `r7` | `fixture-validation` | `b"demo-key=CANARY contact=alex@example.invalid\n"` | $45$ | Secret marker; rejected |

The marker text and address are fictional inputs. Their presence in this table
explains the lesson; it is not permission to include captured secrets or personal
data in a real findings report.

{/* chapter-section:formula */}

## The solution: stop once, count at every reached rule

The fixture deliberately uses small thresholds so each failure is visible:

1. Reject a raw payload above $64$ bytes before decoding it.
2. Reject invalid UTF-8.
3. Normalize the decoded text and reject fewer than $4$ normalized UTF-8 bytes.
4. Reject fewer than $1$ ASCII letter.
5. Reject the literal `demo-key=CANARY`, matched without ASCII case distinctions.
6. Hold the literal `contact=`, matched case-sensitively.
7. Hold text below the configured ASCII-letter share.

Normalization replaces CRLF pairs with LF, then trims only space, tab, CR and LF
at the two edges. It preserves case, internal spaces and other Unicode
characters. Length after normalization is measured in UTF-8 **bytes**, not
characters or tokens.

For the last rule, count Unicode scalar values other than the six ASCII
whitespace characters: space, tab, LF, vertical tab, form feed and CR. The
numerator counts ASCII letters among those values. Compare a configured
fraction using checked integer cross-products, rather than rounding a
floating-point ratio. A zero denominator is unavailable and sends a reached
record to review; it is not an observed share of zero. The fixture's threshold
is $0/1$, so its last survivor passes this rule.

These thresholds are not the full-corpus policy. The planned corpus policy uses
a $65{,}536$-byte raw limit, at least $16$ normalized bytes, at least $8$ ASCII
letters and an ASCII-letter share of at least $1/2$, with its own selected marker
lists. For example, the fixture's short secret record would reach a different
first terminal rule under a stricter length threshold. None of the fixture's
rates are measurements of a real corpus.

For a named rule $k$, report its terminal fraction using the population that
actually reached it:

$$
r_k=\frac{n_{\mathrm{disposition},k}}{n_{\mathrm{seen},k}}
$$

{/* chapter-section:symbol-glossary */}

## Symbols in the filtering fraction

- $k$ identifies a rule in the configured order.
- $n_{\mathrm{seen},k}$ counts records surviving every earlier rule and reaching
  rule $k$.
- $n_{\mathrm{disposition},k}$ counts reached records whose first terminal
  decision is rejection or a hold for review at rule $k$.
- $r_k$ is dimensionless. When $n_{\mathrm{seen},k}=0$, the report stores
  unavailable, not zero.

Four records reach the secret-marker rule, and it rejects two. Its terminal
fraction is $2/4=1/2$. Dividing by the original eight records gives $2/8=1/4$,
a different quantity: that rule's terminal decisions as a fraction of all input
records. Do not label the second quantity as the reached-population rate.

The reached populations are $8,7,6,5,4,2,1$, leaving one retained record.
The final dispositions must conserve the input count:

$$
8=1_{\mathrm{retained}}+6_{\mathrm{rejected}}+1_{\mathrm{manual\ review}}
$$

A binary exclusion summary gives $7$ ineligible records, but those are
$6$ rejections plus $1$ pending review. Calling all seven “rejected” discards
the distinction needed to explain their outcomes.

## Rust owns the framing and decisions

The framer accepts an ordinary `Read` source. The output interface separates
retained rows from body-free exclusion findings, without requiring a directory,
filename, HTTP source or storage backend. Supporting libraries provide JSON
encoding and SHA-256; the course code owns boundaries, rule order, terminal
decisions and accounting.

A bounded buffer retains only payloads within the selected size limit. An
oversized record is drained to its boundary and counted without retaining its
whole body. Read-buffer boundaries do not split records or invalidate a Unicode
character: UTF-8 decoding happens on the complete bounded payload.

  label="Rust source-bound record framing"
/>

The raw source was selected independently before this read. A report succeeds
only after the complete source's observed length and digest agree with that
selection. Rows emitted before that final check are provisional. A changed byte,
truncated read or I/O error prevents publication of the completed result; a
prefix must not become training input.

  label="Rust narrow text normalization"
/>

<RustSource
  path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/filter.rs"

Record `r7` contains both markers. With the secret rule first, it is rejected
there; the manual-marker rule is **not evaluated** for that record. Swap those
two rules and `r7` is held for review instead. The new totals are one retained,
five rejected and two pending review. The same raw bytes therefore produce
different reasons and dispositions under different policies.

<RustSource
  path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/privacy.rs"
  region="literal-marker-decisions"
  caption="Match secret-marker literals without ASCII case distinctions and manual-review literals case-sensitively; neither rule detects all sensitive text."
  label="Rust literal marker matching"
/>

A quoted marker can cause a false positive. Sensitive text without a configured
literal can pass. Likewise, few ASCII letters do not prove that a record is bad
or that it is not English, and many ASCII letters do not establish language or
quality. These heuristics need corpus-specific inspection, including inspection
of excluded text under appropriate access controls.

## Preserve counts without exposing excluded bodies

<RustSource
  path="rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/governance.rs"
  region="stage-accounting"
  caption="Increment a rule's seen count only when the record reaches it, then count survival or its first terminal decision."
  label="Rust reached-population accounting"
/>

A finding contains a source reference, half-open raw byte span, occurrence ID,
evaluated rule IDs and the terminal decision. It contains no excluded body,
snippet or matched capture. The occurrence ID binds the selected raw artifact,
source and payload IDs, raw file digest and span. Equal text at different spans
has different occurrence IDs. A changed filter policy does not change those raw
occurrence IDs, but does change the derived artifact's policy identity.

Per source and terminal reason, the report includes the first $32$ occurrence
IDs in input order as samples. The full finding stream and counters remain
complete: the sample bound is not permission to stop counting. Findings and
the receipt share a strict metadata budget below $100$ MiB. Exceeding that
budget fails the attempt; it does not silently truncate evidence.

Byte accounting uses separate bases. Separator bytes are outside raw payload
spans. Payloads rejected before decoding still contribute to the raw total.
Normalized byte totals include only records actually decoded and normalized.
A complete run reads $287$ physical bytes: $175$ payload bytes and $112$
delimiter bytes. Of the payload bytes, $68$ belong to records rejected before
decoding and $107$ are decoded. Normalization leaves $101$ bytes across decoded
records: $8$ retained, $65$ rejected and $28$ pending review. These are byte
counts, not token counts; excluded text still contributes to its applicable
accounting totals.

A retained row is checked again against the selected filtered artifact, policy,
source references, span and text digest before consumption. Relabeling a
manual-review payload or selecting an untrusted candidate's own manifest does
not make it eligible.

## History: inspect what filtering removes

A binary keep/drop report hides the reason for exclusion and the population that
each later rule actually inspected.

The C4 study examines text removed by filters; RefinedWeb later combines
filtering and deduplication in a web-scale corpus.

Dodge and colleagues inspect C4 exclusions and find disproportionate removal of
content concerning minority groups by its word blocklist. Their 2021
[Documenting Large Webtext Corpora: A Case Study on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.98/)
motivates examining removals rather than assuming that a filter is neutral.

Penedo and colleagues describe a large web corpus built with filtering and
deduplication, and evaluate language models trained on its data. Their 2023
[RefinedWeb paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/fa3ed726cc5073b9c31e3e49a807789c-Abstract-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.html)
concerns a much broader pipeline than this eight-record fixture. Its model
results do not certify our heuristics or isolate a benefit from one rule.

The Rust contrast below is course-local: it reduces our existing decisions to
one exclusion bit. It is not an implementation reproduced from either paper.
It counts seven excluded records but loses their rejection-versus-review
distinction and cannot say which later rule saw each one.

The secret-marker rule's denominator is its four reached records, not all eight

## Optional practice: inspect the recorded evidence

### Source withdrawal is a known-lineage calculation

Filtering also preserves source lineage so a later withdrawal can identify
recorded downstream artifacts. The separate fictional graph uses `r0` as a
**raw-source node alias**, not as the worked table's record label or an actual
occurrence digest. Its descendants are `a0`, `f0`, `s0`, `tok0` and `w0`.
Two paths reach `w0`; the result lists it once. The unrelated branch `f9`
belongs to a different source and is not in this withdrawal's descendant set.

{/* chapter-section:decoder-connection */}

## What continues toward the decoder

Only retained candidates continue to deduplication, final split construction and
tokenization. The candidate set is kept in deterministic source and span order.
Pending-review text cannot join it through a relabeled role or an incomplete
output.

A complete receipt preserves the selected policy, source references and counts.
That makes the filtering decision reproducible, not universally correct. The
scalar decoder remains unchanged, and this small example establishes neither
real-corpus retention rates nor trained-model quality, privacy or memorization
safety.
